opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what I loved most was how fearless Noam was about picking problems. A lot of researchers, especially early on, gravitate toward things that are incremental because they feel safe, and you know you'll get a paper out of it. With Noam it was always, "What's the thing that actually matters? What would change the field if it worked?" And then working backwards from there.

I was really young when we started collaborating, and he just treated me like a peer. We'd go back and forth on ideas, and he'd poke holes in things very directly but never in a discouraging way. It was more like, "Okay, that won't work because of X, but what if we flip it around?" That kind of rapid iteration is incredibly fun, because you're not precious about any single idea. You throw out ten, nine die, and the one that survives is usually much better than what either of you walked in with.

The other thing was his taste. He had this really good intuition for when something was going to scale versus when it was a neat trick that would stay a neat trick. In the poker and imperfect-information game work, there were so many directions you could go, and he had a knack for spotting the ones where, if you just pushed hard enough on compute and search, you'd get a qualitative jump rather than a few percent improvement. That instinct, thinking about what happens when you take an idea seriously and push it all the way, really stuck with me and shaped a lot of how I think about problems today.

And it was just fun. Research can be lonely, and having someone who gets genuinely excited about the same weird problem at midnight makes a huge difference.

fable-5.1.text:
What I loved most about it was that Noam never let me get comfortable with an idea just because it sounded elegant. When we were working on poker and later on the search-and-learning stuff that fed into things like ReBeL, I'd come in excited about some clever algorithmic trick, and his first question was almost always, "Okay, but what is the actual mechanism that makes this work? Where does the advantage come from?" And if I couldn't answer that cleanly, we'd keep going until we either found the mechanism or realized the idea was hollow. That discipline of separating what feels promising from what you can actually explain was incredibly formative for me.

The other thing was just the tempo. We'd go back and forth really quickly, sometimes dozens of half-ideas in an hour, and neither of us was precious about any of them. Something I threw out would get torn apart, he'd rebuild part of it, I'd flip it around again, and by the end you genuinely couldn't say whose idea it was. That's the best kind of collaboration, where the ownership dissolves and you're both just chasing the thing. And he was very generous in that process. I was pretty young at the time, and he treated my objections as seriously as his own, which gave me a lot of confidence that research is really about the quality of the argument rather than the seniority of the person making it.

And honestly, I think it taught me how to think about ambition properly. Noam was always asking what the version of a problem was that actually mattered, not the toy version that was convenient to publish. That instinct to aim at the real target even when it's harder is something I try to carry into everything we do at Magic now.

astra-6.text: What I loved was how quickly we could get to the core of a problem. We could take an idea seriously without getting attached to it: What’s the actual bottleneck? What would have to be true for this to work? And what’s the simplest experiment that would tell us whether we’re onto something? That combination of ambition and willingness to question every assumption made brainstorming really fun.
